sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Patients receiving immune-directed chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy experience profound, prolonged immunosuppression, predisposing them to opportunistic infections. Disseminated angioinvasive Fusarium infections are uncommon but carry high morbidity and mortality in this population.

sec.title: Case Presentation
sec.p: We describe a rare case of disseminated angioinvasive Fusarium infection in a patient with refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma following CD19-directed CAR-T-cell therapy. The patient developed progressive cutaneous lesions due to Fusarium keratoplasticum complex, confirmed by tissue culture and histopathology. She ultimately expired due to septic shock complicated by multifactorial cardiotoxicity.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This case highlights the heightened susceptibility to refractory opportunistic mold infections and potential cardiac complications in patients after CAR-T therapy. New skin lesions in the post-CAR-T period should prompt early biopsy and skin culture with prompt mold coverage.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Fusarium species are filamentous molds found in soil and plant material that can cause opportunistic infections in severely immunocompromised hosts. Disseminated fusariosis is a rare but often fatal infection characterized by angioinvasion, tissue necrosis, and hematogenous dissemination. Historically, it has been described in patients with prolonged neutropenia, hematologic malignancies, or stem cell transplantation [1]. However, this case emphasizes the expanding risk profile in the era of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy.

sec.title: Case Report
sec.p: A 39-year-old woman with refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, non-germinal center subtype with CNS involvement, presented with great toe cellulitis and multiple erythematous nodular skin lesions 2 months after receiving CD19-directed CAR-T therapy. Her medical history included six lines of chemotherapy and autologous CD19-directed CAR-T-cell therapy complicated by grade 2 cytokine release syndrome and neutropenic fevers on day 4 post-CAR-T. She never achieved remission following CAR-T-cell therapy with 85% bone marrow involvement at 30 days post-treatment and persistent pancytopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 0.1 ×109/L). Chemotherapy following CAR-T infusion was notable for a single dose of loncastuximab, and she did not receive radiation at any point during her course of treatment. The patient’s full course of treatment is provided in Figure 1. She had been on appropriate yeast-active prophylaxis with fluconazole and anti-viral prophylaxis with acyclovir. On admission, vital signs revealed a temperature of 37.7°C, tachycardia (HR 111 bpm), and oxygen saturation of 93% on room air. She had scattered petechiae and ecchymoses and erythema and warmth of the right great toe streaking to her midfoot. Laboratory data showed leukopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 0.2 ×109/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 10 ×109/L), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (995 U/L).

caption.p: Timeline summarizing CAR-T infusion, subsequent cytopenias, onset and progression of cutaneous Fusarium lesions, antifungal escalation, cardiac decline, and final hospitalization for septic shock.

sec.p: On the third day of admission, she developed multiple erythematous papulonodular lesions without central necrosis on multiple extremities despite broad spectrum antibiotic coverage for her cellulitis. These subsequently increased in number, involving her other extremities, trunk, scalp, and face (Fig. 2). Punch biopsy of a skin nodule revealed large septate hyphal structures with variable branching angles and spores that were visualized on both hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stains (Fig. 2). Tissue culture grew Fusarium keratoplasticum complex. Antifungal susceptibility testing demonstrated an amphotericin B minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 2 µg/mL and a voriconazole MIC >16 µg/mL without interpretative breakpoints.

caption.p: a Representative image of cutaneous lesions in their early stages. b Progression of cutaneous lesions to violaceous, erythematous, necrotic eschars after 8 days of voriconazole and initiation of amphotericin B. c Initial lesion of the leg (arrow). d Progressive erythema of the same lesion (arrow) over a 3-day course. e Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain showing angioinvasion of spores and sparse hypoid structures. f Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain of the angioinvasive spores confirming fungal origin.

sec.p: Fluconazole prophylaxis was discontinued, and the patient was initiated on IV voriconazole antifungal therapy. Given superficial disease and thrombocytopenia with prolonged bleeding after biopsy, surgical debridement was deferred. Although she initially experienced sufficient stabilization of her cellulitis and Fusarium infection to be discharged with outpatient antibiotics and voriconazole, the patient’s condition deteriorated. On day eight of voriconazole therapy, she re-presented to the hospital meeting 4/4 SIRS criteria (temperature >38.5°C, HR >90 bpm, RR >20, and WBC <4,000/mm3). Antifungal therapy was escalated with the addition of liposomal 5 mg/kg IV amphotericin B. She improved clinically and received 2 doses of intravenous immunoglobulin after 4 days of amphotericin B to improve her treatment response. During her hospitalization, she developed acute high-output heart failure thought to be secondary to sepsis superimposed on chronic anemia and possible subclinical cardiotoxicity from CAR-T-cell therapy (Fig. 3). After 8 days of treatment with liposomal amphotericin B and 16 days of IV voriconazole, she developed hypotension requiring pressor support and ICU management. She ultimately passed away due to multiorgan failure secondary to septic shock surrounded by her friends and family.

caption.p: Global longitudinal strain before and after CAR-T therapy. Pre-CAR-T echocardiogram (May 2025: a, c) demonstrated normal myocardial deformation with global strain (GS) = −19.7% and ejection fraction of 58%. Post-CAR-T echocardiogram (October 2025: b, d) showed reduced strain with GS = −14.3%, indicating new systolic dysfunction with relatively preserved ejection fraction of 56%.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Disseminated Fusarium infection following CAR-T therapy has been reported only rarely. One prior case occurred in a pediatric patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia who had also undergone allogeneic stem cell transplantation, making it difficult to distinguish the relative contributions of CAR-T therapy versus transplant-related immunosuppression [2]. In contrast, our patient developed disseminated fusariosis in the absence of prior stem cell transplantation, which emphasizes the independent risk of opportunistic infections from CAR-T-associated immune dysfunction.

sec.title: Post-CAR-T Immunosuppression and Infection Risk
sec.p: Immune depletion following CD19 CAR-T-cell therapy is primarily driven by profound and sustained B-cell aplasia due to the targeted elimination of CD19+ B cells, resulting in hypogammaglobulinemia and impaired humoral immunity [3]. Although bacterial and viral infections predominate early, opportunistic fungal infections may emerge weeks to months later [4]. While invasive aspergillosis and mucormycosis have been occasionally reported, disseminated Fusarium infection following CAR-T therapy remains exceedingly rare [2, 5–7]. Our case adds to the limited evidence of life-threatening mold infections in this setting, emphasizing several aspects of multifactorial immune dysfunction: neutropenia, lymphodepletion, and B-cell aplasia.

sec.title: Post-CAR-T Cardiotoxicity
sec.p: A notable feature of this case was the acute onset of heart failure, which ultimately contributed to multi-organ failure and cardiovascular collapse secondary to septic shock. The patient had few comorbidities that would predispose her to heart failure. However, her post-CAR-T course had been complicated by grade 2 cytokine release syndrome, and it is plausible that subclinical cardiac dysfunction developed at that time and was unmasked or exacerbated in the setting of sepsis [8]. Patients undergoing CAR-T-cell therapy are exposed to a constellation of cardiac stressors, including but not limited to chronic anemia and cardiotoxic chemotherapies. In this context, it is valuable to monitor for newly developing heart failure, as it significantly worsens outcomes in septic shock, and in this case, may have played a role in the patient’s poor clinical trajectory [9].

sec.title: Diagnostic Considerations
sec.p: The clinical presentation of fusariosis can mimic other molds, particularly Aspergillus [10]. Cutaneous manifestations are common in disseminated disease and often provide an accessible diagnostic window. Positive blood cultures, rare in other filamentous fungi, may also aid early recognition in Fusarium. However, culture confirmation and sensitivities are critical, as empiric mold-active prophylaxis (e.g., posaconazole) may not provide sufficient coverage due to intrinsic resistance patterns [11].

sec.title: Therapeutic Challenges
sec.p: Treatment of disseminated Fusarium infection is difficult, with mortality rates exceeding 80% in neutropenic hosts [12]. Most isolates demonstrate high MICs to azoles, and amphotericin B activity varies by species complex [13]. Combination therapy with amphotericin B and voriconazole or posaconazole is often employed empirically. However, the adverse side effect profile of amphotericin B often prompts hesitation in initiation. In this case, we noted mild cutaneous involvement which progressed rapidly despite treatment with voriconazole. The primary barrier to inpatient administration of amphotericin B in this case was the patient’s strong preference to return home to be with her family, which influenced the decision to pursue discharge once she was clinically stable. Restoration of immune function, particularly neutrophil recovery, remains the most important prognostic factor. In our case, persistent cytopenia after CAR-T therapy despite treatment with G-CSF limited host recovery and likely contributed to her poor outcome.

sec.title: Clinical Implications
sec.p:
This case highlights three important lessons for clinicians managing post-CAR-T patients:1.
Early suspicion and diagnosis: unexplained, clinically suspicious skin lesions in the post-CAR-T period should prompt evaluation for mold infections with lesional biopsy. Importantly, standard fluconazole prophylaxis does not protect against mold infections.2.
Refractory immunosuppression: persistent cytopenias post-CAR-T necessitates ongoing vigilance and high index of suspicion for opportunistic infections.3.
Cardiac monitoring: baseline and follow-up cardiac assessment should be considered in patients with cytokine release syndrome, as early recognition and management of heart failure can influence outcomes in the post-CAR-T setting.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Disseminated angioinvasive Fusarium infection represents a rare, but devastating complication in patients receiving CAR-T therapy. While a lifesaving treatment for some, CAR-T cell therapy confers a long-term and multifactorial immune impairment that is thought to be similar in nature to that of transplant recipients and differing significantly from conventional transient chemotherapy toxicity. Future strategies for optimal post-CAR-T management may require combination antifungal therapy and, when feasible, immune reconstitution strategies [14].

sec.title: Words from Our Patient
sec.p: On discussion with the patient regarding the use of her clinical information for a case report, she was enthusiastic about the opportunity to contribute to medical education. She wanted those reading her story to know that if she couldn’t be cured, she would want a cure for the next person. She instructed the authors to “learn, learn, learn.”
